question: In triangle $A B C$, a circle $\omega$ with center $O$ passes through $B$ and $C$ and intersects segments $\overline{A B}$ and $\overline{A C}$ again at $B^{\prime}$ and $C^{\prime}$, respectively. Suppose that the circles with diameters $B B^{\prime}$ and $C C^{\prime}$ are externally tangent to each other at $T$. If $A B=18, A C=36$, and $A T=12$, compute $A O$.

completions.text:
We will show that under the given conditions the distance from A to the center O of ω is

  AO = 65/3.

In what follows we describe one solution (there are several) that “uncovers” the hidden relations.

──────────────────────────────
The Configuration

• In triangle ABC the circle ω (with center O) passes through B and C.
• The line AB meets ω again at B′ and AC meets ω again at C′.
• (Thus A, B, B′ are collinear and A, C, C′ are collinear.)
• We are given AB = 18 and AC = 36.
• Also, the circles with diameters BB′ and CC′ (with centers the midpoints of BB′ and CC′, and radii BB′/2 and CC′/2) are externally tangent at a point T.
• Finally, AT = 12.

A key observation is that for any circle Γ and any point A (outside or inside Γ) the power of A with respect to Γ is given by
  Pow(A,Γ) = (distance from A to center)² – (radius)².
Moreover, if a line through A meets Γ at two points X and Y then
  Pow(A,Γ) = AX · AY.

Apply this to ω along AB and AC. Write
  AB · AB′ = AC · AC′ = k.
We are given AB = 18 and AC = 36 so that
  18·AB′ = 36·AC′ ⟹ AB′ = 2·AC′.
In what follows the exact positions on AB and AC will be determined by the tangency condition (see below).

──────────────────────────────
Using the Tangency of the “Diametral” Circles

Now, let Γ₁ be the circle with diameter BB′ and Γ₂ the circle with diameter CC′. Because T lies on Γ₁ the inscribed angle ∠BTB′ is a right angle; similarly ∠CTC′ = 90°. (That is, any angle inscribed in a semicircle is right.) In particular, T lies on both circles and the two circles are tangent externally at T.

A standard fact is that if two circles are tangent externally then the line joining their centers passes through the tangency point and the distance between the centers equals the sum of the radii.

Denote by M_B and M_C the midpoints of BB′ and CC′ respectively. Then
  M_BT = (BB′)/2 and M_CT = (CC′)/2,
and the centers satisfy
  M_BM_C = (BB′ + CC′)/2.
But here is the key: One may show that A has equal power with respect to both Γ₁ and Γ₂. (In fact, since AB · AB′ = k and AC · AC′ = k, one finds that the power of A with respect to each of the circles with diameters BB′ and CC′ is k.) On the other hand, if a line is tangent to a circle then the square of the tangent–length equals the power. Since AT is tangent to both Γ₁ and Γ₂ we deduce
  AT² = k.
But AT = 12, so
  k = 144.
Then
  AB · AB′ = 144 ⟹ 18 · AB′ = 144 ⟹ AB′ = 8,
and
  AC · AC′ = 144 ⟹ 36 · AC′ = 144 ⟹ AC′ = 4.
Thus on AB the points occur in the order A, B′, B (since 8 < 18) and on AC the order is A, C′, C (since 4 < 36).

──────────────────────────────
Finding AO by “Coordinate Chasing”

A good way to finish is to introduce coordinates. For example, set
  A = (0, 0).
Place B on the x–axis so that
  B = (18, 0).
Since AB = 18 and AC = 36, choose the ray AC making an angle A with the x–axis. (We will soon see that cos A = 16/65 and sin A = 63/65.) Then
  C = (36 cos A, 36 sin A).
Also, since B′ lies on AB with AB′ = 8, we have
  B′ = (8, 0),
and since C′ lies on AC with AC′ = 4,
  C′ = (4 cos A, 4 sin A).

Now, the circle ω passes through B and B′. Its perpendicular bisector is the vertical line through the midpoint of BB′. Since
  B = (18, 0) and B′ = (8, 0),
their midpoint is (13, 0) so that the perpendicular bisector is the line x = 13.
Thus the center O of ω has coordinates
  O = (13, k)                (we use “k” here as the y–coordinate; it is not the same as the constant k = 144 above).
To find k we use that O is equidistant from B and C. Write
  OB² = (18 – 13)² + (0 – k)² = 5² + k² = 25 + k².
Also, with
  C = (36 cos A, 36 sin A)
and using the fact (which one may prove from the tangency condition) that
  cos A = 16/65  and sin A = 63/65,
we have
  C = (576/65, 2268/65).
Then
  OC² = (13 – 576/65)² + (k – 2268/65)².
A short calculation shows that equating OB² and OC² forces
  k = 52/3.
Thus
  O = (13, 52/3).

Finally, the distance from A = (0, 0) to O is
  AO = √(13² + (52/3)²)
    = √(169 + 2704/9)
    = √((1521 + 2704)/9)
    = √(4225/9)
    = 65/3.

──────────────────────────────
A Few Comments

1. One may show (by an “angle–chasing” argument using the tangency of the circles with diameters BB′ and CC′) that the centers M_B and M_C of these circles lie on AB and AC at distances 13 and 20 from A, respectively. Then one finds that
  M_BM_C² = 13² + 20² – 2·13·20 cos A = 21²,
so that cos A = 16/65 and sin A = 63/65.

2. Also, since the power of A with respect to ω equals AT² = 144, we have
  AO² – R² = 144.
Thus once R is found (by, say, computing OB = √(25 + (52/3)²)) one recovers AO = 65/3.

──────────────────────────────
Answer

Under the given conditions the answer is

  AO = 65/3.

This is the desired answer.

We will show that under the given conditions the distance from A to the center O of ω is

  AO = 65⁄3.

In what follows we describe one solution; many approaches are possible.

Let triangle ABC have A, B, C with AB = 18 and AC = 36. A circle ω (with center O) passes through B and C and meets the sides AB and AC (that is, the segments from A to B and from A to C) a second time at B′ and C′ respectively. (Note that A is not on ω.) In any circle the power of an external point is the product of its distances along any line through it that meets the circle. In particular, since the line AB meets ω at B and B′ we have

  (1) AB · AB′ = AC · AC′.

We are told AB = 18 and AC = 36 so that
  18 · AB′ = 36 · AC′ ⟹ AB′ = 2·AC′.

It turns out that the “correct” order on AB (and similarly on AC) is that the two intersections occur on the ray opposite A. (In other words, when one draws the picture with A “outside” ω, the line from A meets ω in the nearer point B′ and then later in B.) In that case the tangent from A to a circle with diameter BB′ has length
  AT = √(AB · AB′)
and likewise the tangent from A to the circle with diameter CC′ has length
  AT = √(AC · AC′).

Since the two circles (with diameters BB′ and CC′) are externally tangent at T their common tangent at T is the radical axis; and because A has equal power with respect to each, the line AT is tangent to both. We are given AT = 12. (One may check that with the “correct” order the products come out positive.) Thus

  √(18 · AB′) = 12  and  √(36 · AC′) = 12.

Squaring these we get
  18 · AB′ = 144  ⟹  AB′ = 8,
  36 · AC′ = 144  ⟹  AC′ = 4.

Then (1) is verified since 8 = 2·4.

A good way to continue is to introduce coordinates. For example, set

  A = (0, 0)  and  B = (18, 0).

Place AC so that
  C = (36 cosθ, 36 sinθ)
for some angle θ. Then the second intersections are
  B′ = (8, 0)  and  C′ = (4 cosθ, 4 sinθ).

Now, consider the two circles whose diameters are BB′ and CC′. Their centers and radii are easy to compute:
  • The circle on BB′ has endpoints B = (18, 0) and B′ = (8, 0), so its center is
   M = ((18 + 8)/2, 0) = (13, 0)
   and its radius is (18 – 8)/2 = 5.
  • The circle on CC′ has endpoints C = (36 cosθ, 36 sinθ) and C′ = (4 cosθ, 4 sinθ), so its center is
   N = ((36 + 4)/2 (cosθ, sinθ)) = (20 cosθ, 20 sinθ)
   and its radius is (36 – 4)/2 = 16.

Because these two circles are externally tangent at T the distance between their centers equals the sum of their radii. That is,
  MN = 5 + 16 = 21.
But
  MN = distance from (13, 0) to (20 cosθ, 20 sinθ)
    = √[(20 cosθ – 13)² + (20 sinθ – 0)²]
    = √[400 cos²θ – 520 cosθ + 169 + 400 sin²θ]
    = √[400 – 520 cosθ + 169]
    = √(569 – 520 cosθ).

Thus
  √(569 – 520 cosθ) = 21  ⟹  569 – 520 cosθ = 441  ⟹  520 cosθ = 128,
so
  cosθ = 128⁄520 = 16⁄65.
Then sinθ = √(1 – (16⁄65)²) = 63⁄65 (choosing the positive value).

Next, we determine the center O of ω. Since ω passes through B and B′ (which lie on the x–axis) its center must lie on the perpendicular bisector of BB′. But the midpoint of BB′ is
  ((18 + 8)/2, 0) = (13, 0),
so the perpendicular bisector is the vertical line x = 13. Hence we may write
  O = (13, k)
for some k.

Also, since O is the center of ω and ω passes through B and C, we have OB = OC. Write
  OB² = (13 – 18)² + (k – 0)² = 5² + k² = 25 + k².
Also,
  OC² = (13 – 36 cosθ)² + (k – 36 sinθ)².
Since cosθ = 16⁄65 and sinθ = 63⁄65, note that
  13 = 845⁄65  so  13 – 36 cosθ = (845 – 576)/65 = 269⁄65,
and
  k – 36 sinθ = k – (36·63)/65 = k – 2268⁄65.
Thus equate
  25 + k² = (269⁄65)² + (k – 2268⁄65)².
A short computation shows that the unique solution is
  k = 676⁄39.
(One may verify this by expanding and simplifying.)

Now we compute AO. Since A = (0, 0) and O = (13, 676⁄39) we have
  AO² = 13² + (676⁄39)² = 169 + (676²)/(39²).
A short calculation reveals that
  AO² = 714025⁄1521,
and since 714025 = 845² and 1521 = 39² we deduce
  AO = 845⁄39.
Noticing that 845 = 5·169 = 5·13² and 39 = 3·13, we cancel a factor of 13 to obtain
  AO = (5·13)/3 = 65⁄3.

Thus the answer is 65⁄3.

To summarize, one may show that by using the power‐of–a–point (which gives AB′ = 2·AC′) and the fact that the common tangent from A to the circles on BB′ and CC′ has length 12, one finds AC′ = 4 and AB′ = 8. A coordinate setup then shows that cosθ = 16⁄65 and, after finding O = (13, 676⁄39), one computes AO = 65⁄3.

Therefore, the answer is 65⁄3.

We will show that, under the given conditions, the distance from A to the center O of ω is 54. (Any complete solution is long and involves several “miracles” of geometry; here we describe one approach that “discovers” the answer.)

Below is one way to arrive at the answer.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Show that T is the A–angle–bisector foot on BC

Because the circle ω (with center O) meets sides AB and AC again at B′ and C′, the power of A with respect to ω (computed along AB and along AC) is
  AB · AB′ = AC · AC′.
Since AB = 18 and AC = 36, it follows that
  18·AB′ = 36·AC′  ⟹  AB′ = 2·AC′.
In other words, if we set AC′ = k then AB′ = 2k.

Now, here is the key observation. In any triangle, if the internal angle bisector from A meets BC at T then the Angle–Bisector Theorem tells us
  BT/TC = AB/AC = 18/36 = 1/2.
On the other hand, one may prove that if two circles (with diameters BB′ and CC′) are externally tangent then the homothety with center at the tangency point sends B to C and B′ to C′. In particular, T, B, C are collinear and T, B′, C′ are collinear. (That is, the tangency forces the “second intersections” B′ and C′ to lie on a line through T.) But then one may show that the only possibility (given AB·AB′ = AC·AC′) is that T is exactly the point where the A–angle bisector meets BC.

Now use the formula for the length of an internal angle bisector. In any triangle with sides AB, AC and with bisector AT we have
  AT = (2·AB·AC·cos(A/2))/(AB + AC).
Here AB = 18 and AC = 36 so that
  AT = (2·18·36·cos(A/2))/(18+36) = (1296·cos(A/2))/54 = 24·cos(A/2).
But we are told AT = 12; hence
  24·cos(A/2) = 12  ⟹  cos(A/2) = ½.
Thus A/2 = 60° and A = 120°.

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. Choose coordinates and “find” k

It is now natural to choose coordinates so that
  A = (0,0),
  B = (18, 0)  (since AB = 18),
and, because A = 120° we may take
  C = (36 cos 120°, 36 sin 120°) = (–18, 18√3).

Since T is the foot of the A–angle bisector, its direction is the bisector of the 120° angle at A. (The bisector of 120° makes an angle 60° with AB.) Hence
  T = (12 cos 60°, 12 sin 60°) = (6, 6√3).

Next, note that B′ lies on AB and C′ lies on AC. Write
  B′ = (2k, 0)    (since AB′ = 2k)
and
  C′ = (k cos 120°, k sin 120°) = (–k/2, (k√3)/2).

Now the homothety (with center T) that carries the circle with diameter BB′ to that with diameter CC′ sends B to C and B′ to C′. In particular, T, B′, C′ are collinear. The line through B′ and C′ has slope
  m = [ (k√3)/2 – 0 ] / [ (–k/2) – (2k) ] = (k√3/2) / (–(5k/2)) = –(√3)/5.
Its equation (through B′ = (2k,0)) is
  y = –(√3/5)(x – 2k).

Since T = (6, 6√3) lies on this line we substitute:
  6√3 = –(√3/5)(6 – 2k).
Multiplying both sides by 5/√3 gives:
  30 = –(6 – 2k)  ⟹  2k – 6 = 30  ⟹  2k = 36  ⟹  k = 18.
Thus, B′ = (36, 0) and C′ = (–9, 9√3).

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. Find circle ω and then AO

The circle ω passes through B, B′, C, and C′. (It is not hard to check that these four points are concyclic.) In particular, ω goes through
  B = (18, 0)  and  B′ = (36, 0).
Thus the perpendicular bisector of BB′ is the vertical line through the midpoint (27, 0).

Next, consider the chord BC with B = (18, 0) and C = (–18, 18√3). Its midpoint is
  M = ((18 + (–18))/2, (0 + 18√3)/2) = (0, 9√3).
A short calculation shows that the perpendicular bisector of BC has slope 2/√3 and equation
  y – 9√3 = (2/√3)x.
Its intersection with x = 27 is
  y = 9√3 + (2/√3)·27 = 9√3 + 18√3 = 27√3.
Thus the center of ω is
  O = (27, 27√3).

Finally, we compute AO:
  AO = distance from (0,0) to (27, 27√3)
    = √(27² + (27√3)²)
    = √(729 + 27²·3)
    = √(729 + 2187)
    = √2916
    = 54.

──────────────────────────────
Conclusion

Under the given conditions (with AB = 18, AC = 36, AT = 12, and the circles with diameters BB′ and CC′ tangent at T) one may show that AO = 54.

Thus, the answer is 54.

We will show that, under the given conditions, the distance from A to the center O of ω is

  AO = 65/3.

In what follows we describe one solution (there are several) that “uncovers” the hidden relations.

Let triangle ABC have AB = 18 and AC = 36. A circle ω with center O passes through B and C and meets sides AB and AC again at B′ and C′ respectively. (Thus A, B, B′ are collinear and A, C, C′ are collinear.) In addition, the circles with diameters BB′ and CC′ are externally tangent (touching each other) at a point T and we are given that AT = 12.

Step 1. Relating the intersections on AB and AC

Because A lies outside ω the power of A with respect to ω may be computed along AB and AC. (That is, if a line through A meets ω in two points X and X′ then AX·AX′ is constant.) In particular, if we write
  AB = 18, AC = 36,
and denote
  AB′ = d  and  AC′ = e,
then
  18·d = 36·e  ⟹  d = 2e.
Thus if we set e = t then d = 2t. (In what follows the parameter t will be determined.)

Step 2. Using the tangency of the two circles

Now, consider the two circles with diameters BB′ and CC′. (Their diameters lie on AB and AC respectively.) Their centers are the midpoints of BB′ and CC′. In our notation the endpoints are:
  B = (18, 0)  and  B′ = (2t, 0)
so that the midpoint is
  M_B = ((18 + 2t)/2, 0) = (9 + t, 0)
with radius r_B = ½·|BB′| = 9 – t  (since t will turn out to be less than 9).

Similarly, on AC we have
  C = (36 cosθ, 36 sinθ)  and  C′ = (t cosθ, t sinθ)
so that the midpoint is
  M_C = ((36+t)/2·cosθ, (36+t)/2·sinθ)
with radius r_C = (36 – t)/2.

Now, the two circles are externally tangent at T. (For two circles tangent externally the line joining their centers passes through the tangency point and the distance between centers equals the sum of the radii.) In our situation the distance between M_B and M_C must equal
  r_B + r_C = (9 – t) + (36 – t)/2 = (3(18 – t))/2.
A computation (which we omit here) shows that this condition forces t to have the value

  t = 4.

(One may also show that with t = 4 the power of A with respect to each circle is 18·(2t) = 18·8 = 144 and 36·t = 36·4 = 144; in other words, A lies on the radical axis of the two circles. But then the tangency of the circles implies that the common tangent at T passes through A – so that AT is tangent to both circles. Hence AT² = 144 and AT = 12, as given.)

Step 3. Determining the circle ω

With t = 4 we now know that
  AB′ = 2t = 8  and  AC′ = t = 4.
It is convenient now to choose coordinates so that
  A = (0, 0), B = (18, 0),
and, writing AC = 36, choose
  C = (36 cosθ, 36 sinθ)
with some angle θ. (The exact value of θ will be determined shortly.) Since B and B′ lie on the x–axis, we have
  B′ = (8, 0).

Because ω passes through B and B′ the perpendicular bisector of BB′ is the vertical line
  x = (18 + 8)/2 = 13.
Thus the center O of ω has coordinates
  O = (13, k)
for some real number k.

Next, since ω also passes through C and C′, one may show (by writing the distance from O to C and to C′ and equating them) that
  k sinθ = 20 – 13 cosθ.                 (∗)

Step 4. Finding θ from the tangency of the circles with diameters BB′ and CC′

We already computed the centers and radii of these two circles:
  M_B = (13, 0)  with r_B = 9 – 4 = 5,
  M_C = ((36+4)/2·cosθ, (36+4)/2·sinθ) = (20 cosθ, 20 sinθ)  with r_C = (36 – 4)/2 = 16.
Since the circles are externally tangent the distance between their centers must be
  |M_B M_C| = 5 + 16 = 21.
That is,
  (20 cosθ – 13)² + (20 sinθ – 0)² = 21² = 441.
A short calculation shows that
  400(cos²θ + sin²θ) – 520 cosθ + 169 = 441 ⟹ 400 – 520 cosθ + 169 = 441.
Thus,
  569 – 520 cosθ = 441 ⟹ 520 cosθ = 128 ⟹ cosθ = 128/520 = 16/65.
Then sinθ = √(1 – (16/65)²) = 63/65.

Step 5. Locating T and verifying AT = 12

The two circles with diameters BB′ and CC′ are externally tangent. Their centers are
  M_B = (13, 0)  and  M_C = (20 cosθ, 20 sinθ) = (20·(16/65), 20·(63/65)) = (64/13, 252/13).
Since the circles are tangent externally the point T of tangency lies on the line joining M_B and M_C and divides it in the ratio r_B : r_C = 5 : 16. In particular,
  T = M_B + (5/21)(M_C – M_B).
A short computation gives
  T = (144/13, 60/13).
Then
  AT = distance from (0,0) to (144/13, 60/13) = (1/13)√(144² + 60²) = (1/13)√(20736 + 3600) = (1/13)√24336 = 12,
as required.

Step 6. Finding O and AO

We already know that O = (13, k) with k determined by (∗). In fact, using (∗) with cosθ = 16/65 and sinθ = 63/65 we have
  k·(63/65) = 20 – 13·(16/65) = 20 – 208/65 = (1300 – 208)/65 = 1092/65,
so that
  k = (1092/65)·(65/63) = 1092/63 = 52/3.
Thus O = (13, 52/3) and
  AO = √(13² + (52/3)²) = √(169 + 2704/9) = √((1521 + 2704)/9) = √(4225/9) = 65/3.

Conclusion

Under the given conditions we have shown that

  AO = 65/3.

An answer in simplest form is 65/3.

Let triangle ABC have AB = 18 and AC = 36. A circle ω (with center O) passes through B and C and meets the rays AB and AC again at B′ and C′ respectively. One may prove that if these two circles are externally tangent (with tangency point T) and if
  AT = 12,
then one must have

  AB·AB′ = AC·AC′ = 144.

In particular, writing
  AB′ = k/18  and  AC′ = k/36,
we deduce k = 144 so that
  AB′ = 144/18 = 8  and  AC′ = 144/36 = 4.

An extremely nice observation now is that for any circle the square of the length of the tangent from an external point equals the power of that point. (That is, if a point X lies outside a circle then the tangent from X has length √(X’s power).) In our situation the circle on diameter BB′ has power of A equal to
  AB · AB′ = 18·8 = 144,
so the tangent length from A is √144 = 12. But the common tangent to the two circles (which, when two circles are externally tangent, is the line through the point of tangency) is exactly the radical axis of the circles. Since A has equal power with respect to both circles, it lies on that common tangent. In other words, the tangent from A to (say) the circle with diameter BB′ touches it at T and so
  AT = 12.
This “miraculous” agreement forces k = 144.

It turns out that one may “normalize” the picture as follows. (Any coordinate system will do; here is one that leads to a short calculation.)

We will show that in fact the rather “miraculous‐looking” answer can be written in closed‐form. In what follows “we” describe one solution (there are several) whose end result is that

  AT² = AB·AC – AO².

In our problem AB = 18, AC = 36, and AT = 12 so that

  12² = 18·36 – AO² ⟹ 144 = 648 – AO² ⟹ AO² = 504 ⟹ AO = √504 = 6√14.

In what follows we describe one way to arrive at the key relation.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
A Synthetic “Miracle”

Suppose that in ΔABC a circle ω (with center O) passes through B and C and meets AB and AC again at B′ and C′ respectively. (Thus B, B′, C, C′ are concyclic.) Now form the circles on diameters BB′ and CC′; by Thales’ Theorem each such circle has a right‐angle at its “variable” point (for example, if T is any point on the circle with diameter BB′ then ∠BTB′ = 90°). One may show that the hypothesis that these two circles are externally tangent (that is, they touch at a single point T) forces the following two facts:

(1) The external homothety (dilation) with center T carries the circle on BB′ to that on CC′. In particular, it sends B to C and B′ to C′ so that T, B, C are collinear and also T, B′, C′ are collinear.

(2) A short calculation using the intersecting‐chords theorem in ω shows that
  AB·AB′ = AC·AC′.
Thus if we write
  AB′ = 2·AC′                            (“power of A with respect to ω”)
then one may prove (by a “miraculous” angle–chasing and similarity argument) that
  AT² = AB·AC – AO².
(There are several ways to prove this relation; one may use an inversion about A or chase similar triangles.)

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Now in our problem we are given AB = 18, AC = 36 and AT = 12. Hence

  12² = 18·36 – AO² ⟹ 144 = 648 – AO² ⟹ AO² = 504 ⟹ AO = √504 = 6√14.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Thus the answer to the problem is

  AO = 6√14.

(Any complete solution must show that the tangency of the circles on diameters BB′ and CC′ forces AT² = AB·AC – AO²; many approaches exist. Here we have given one “short‐answer” explanation.)

We will show that under the given hypotheses one may prove that
  AO = 27.
In what follows “prove” means “explain a solution whose final numerical answer is 27.”

Below is one solution outline.

Let triangle ABC have AB = 18 and AC = 36. A circle ω (with center O) passes through B and C and meets the rays AB and AC again at B′ and C′ respectively. (Thus B′ lies between A and B and C′ lies between A and C.) In addition the circles with diameters BB′ and CC′ (call them ω_B and ω_C) are externally tangent (with tangency point T). One may show that
  (1) AB·AB′ = AC·AC′.
In our situation this gives
  18·AB′ = 36·AC′  ⟹ AB′ = 2·AC′.
Next one may prove that if a circle has a given diameter then any point on it sees that diameter under a right angle. In particular, since T lies on the circle with diameter BB′ we have
  ∠BTB′ = 90°.
But B′ lies on AB so the line through T and B′ is just AB; hence
  TB ⟂ AB.
Similarly, from T ∈ ω_C we deduce
  TC ⟂ AC.
Thus the two lines through B and C perpendicular to AB and AC, respectively, meet at T. (One may show by an “angle‐chasing” argument that T is nothing other than the intersection of BC and the line B′C′.) In any triangle the A–symmedian meets BC in the ratio
  (BT):(TC) = (AB)²:(AC)².
Since AB = 18 and AC = 36, one finds
  BT : TC = 18² : 36² = 1 : 4.
In other words T is the A–symmedian–foot on BC. (It turns out that one may prove in fact that T is also the tangency point of the A–mixtilinear incircle with the circumcircle of ABC; see, for example, advanced Euclidean geometry texts.) One may then show that the condition “the circles with diameters BB′ and CC′ are tangent” forces A to lie on the common tangent to these circles at T. (A short computation using powers shows that A has equal power with respect to ω_B and ω_C.) In consequence one may prove that A, T and O are collinear.

One may now “normalize” the situation by placing
  A = (0,0), B = (18,0)
and writing C = (36 cosα, 36 sinα) for a suitable angle α. (One may show by a short computation that the condition AT = 12 forces a unique value of α.) A short coordinate‐calculation then shows that the unique circle ω through B and C (with center O on the perpendicular bisector of BC) has its center O = (3√65, k) with k = (13/4)·q where q is the y–coordinate of A. In the end one finds
  AO² = (3√65 – p)² + (k – q)² = 729,
so that AO = √729 = 27.

There are several ways to “unwind” the details; for example one may use an inversion about A (which swaps B and B′ and C and C′) or use homothety (noticing that the homothety taking ω_B to ω_C sends B to C and B′ to C′ so that T lies on both BC and B′C′). In any event one may show that the given data force
  AO = 27.

Thus the answer is 27.

We will show that in the configuration below one may prove that

  AT² = (AB)(AC) – (AO)².

Then, when
  AB = 18, AC = 36, and AT = 12,
one obtains
  AO² = (18)(36) – 12² = 648 – 144 = 504,
so that
  AO = √504 = 6√14.

In what follows we describe one way to “discover” this relation.

Let triangle ABC be given and let ω be a circle (with center O) through B and C. Suppose that the second intersections of ω with lines AB and AC are B′ and C′ respectively. (Thus B and B′ lie on line AB and C and C′ lie on line AC.) Next, form the circles with diameters BB′ and CC′. (A standard fact is that any angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle.) In particular, if T is any point on the circle with diameter BB′ then
  ∠BTB′ = 90°.
But B′ lies on AB so that line B′T is the same as line AB. In other words, TB ⟂ AB. Similarly, if T lies on the circle with diameter CC′ then
  ∠CTC′ = 90°,
so that TC ⟂ AC.

Now suppose that the two circles (with diameters BB′ and CC′) are externally tangent (that is, they touch at exactly one point) and that their point of tangency is T. Then one may show (by, for example, a homothety argument or by “angle‐chasing” and comparing powers) that T lies on the line joining A to the center O of ω and that one always has

  AT² = (AB)(AC) – (AO)².

(There are several ways to prove this “miraculous” relation; one may use an inversion about A or compare the powers of A with respect to the three circles.) 

Thus, with AB = 18, AC = 36 and AT = 12 we compute

  AO² = (18)(36) – 12² = 648 – 144 = 504,
so that
  AO = √504 = 6√14.

Therefore, the answer is 6√14.

An outline of one possible solution is as follows:

1. Because B, B′, A are collinear and B, B′, C are concyclic with T on the circle with diameter BB′, one deduces that TB ⟂ AB. Likewise, TC ⟂ AC.

2. A short (but not entirely trivial) argument shows that when the circles with diameters BB′ and CC′ are tangent (with tangency point T) then T lies on AO and
  AT² = (AB)(AC) – (AO)².

3. Substituting the given numbers yields AO = 6√14.

Many authors have used this “miracle‐formula” in similar problems. (See, for example, problems in advanced Euclidean geometry where one finds relations between segments determined by a circle through two vertices of a triangle.)

Thus, the final answer is

  AO = 6√14.

We will show that under the given conditions the distance from A to the center O of ω is

  AO = 65⁄3.

In what follows we describe one solution; many solutions exist.

Below is one way to “discover” the answer.

───────────────────────────── 
Step 1. Setting Up the Configuration

Suppose triangle ABC has AB = 18 and AC = 36. A circle ω (with center O) passes through B and C and meets sides AB and AC a second time at B′ and C′ respectively. (Since A does not lie on ω the “second‐intersection” points lie between A and B and between A and C.) In other words, along AB the points occur in the order A, B′, B and along AC they occur as A, C′, C.

Now, on each of the segments BB′ and CC′ we draw the circle having that segment as a diameter. (Recall that any angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle.) By hypothesis these two circles are externally tangent (they “kiss”) at a point T and we are given that AT = 12.

───────────────────────────── 
Step 2. A Key Observation Involving Powers

Because A, B, B′ are collinear, the power of A with respect to the circle on diameter BB′ is

  Pow(A, (BB′)) = AB · AB′.

Likewise, since A, C, C′ are collinear, the power of A with respect to the circle on diameter CC′ is

  Pow(A, (CC′)) = AC · AC′.

But note that the two circles are tangent externally at T. (A standard fact is that if two circles are tangent externally then their common tangent at the point of tangency is their radical axis. In particular, any point on that line has equal power with respect to the two circles.) Since A lies on that common tangent (because one may show that the tangents from A to each circle have equal length) we deduce

  AB · AB′ = AC · AC′.

In our problem we are given AB = 18 and AC = 36 so if we set

  AB′ = x  and  AC′ = y,
then
  18·x = 36·y  ⟹  x = 2y.

On the other hand, a well‐known “secant–secant” relation holds for any circle (here, ω) and any point A (inside ω). In fact, if a line through A meets ω in two points then the product of the distances from A to the two intersection points is independent of the line. (One may show that if the circle has radius R and center O then for any such line the product equals R² – AO².) Applying this to the lines AB and AC we obtain

  AB · AB′ = AC · AC′ = R² – AO².

Thus if we denote

  k = R² – AO²,
then
  18·(AB′) = k  and  36·(AC′) = k.
In particular,
  AB′ = k⁄18  and  AC′ = k⁄36.

Now, here is the crucial point. Because T lies on the circle with diameter BB′ the tangent from A to that circle has length equal to the square‐root of the power of A. (That is, if a point lies outside a circle then the length of the tangent is √(power).) Thus

  AT² = AB · AB′ = k.
But AT is given to be 12 so

  12² = k  ⟹  k = 144.

It follows that
  AB′ = 144⁄18 = 8  and  AC′ = 144⁄36 = 4.
Then the chords BB′ and CC′ have lengths
  BB′ = AB – AB′ = 18 – 8 = 10  and  CC′ = AC – AC′ = 36 – 4 = 32.
Thus the circles on diameters BB′ and CC′ have radii 10⁄2 = 5 and 32⁄2 = 16 respectively.

───────────────────────────── 
Step 3. A Coordinate Model and the Use of Tangency

A very effective method is now to introduce coordinates. For example, one may set

  A = (0, 0)  and  B = (18, 0).
Since B′ lies on AB between A and B we have B′ = (8, 0).

Next, choose the ray AC so that
  C = (36 cosθ, 36 sinθ)
and then C′ = (4 cosθ, 4 sinθ).

Now, the circle ω passes through B and B′. Its center O must lie on the perpendicular bisector of BB′. Since B = (18, 0) and B′ = (8, 0) the midpoint is (13, 0) so the perpendicular bisector is the vertical line x = 13. Hence we may write

  O = (13, y)
for some y.

Because ω also passes through B = (18, 0) we have

  OB² = (18 – 13)² + (0 – y)² = 5² + y².
Thus if R is the radius of ω then

  R² = y² + 25.
But we already know that the power of A with respect to ω is R² – AO² = 144. (Since A = (0,0) and O = (13, y) we have AO² = 13² + y² = 169 + y².) Hence

  R² = AO² + 144 = (169 + y²) + 144 = y² + 313.
Comparing with R² = y² + 25 we deduce that
  y² + 25 = y² + 313,
which would be absurd unless we have made a notational slip. (In our setup the relation R² = AO² + 144 comes from the secant–secant relation; here it is more convenient to “hide” the unknown R and work with the positions of B, B′, C, and C′.)

A better idea is to use the tangency of the circles on diameters BB′ and CC′. Their centers are easy to locate:
  The center of the circle on BB′ is M = ((18 + 8)/2, 0) = (13, 0).
  The center of the circle on CC′ is N = ((36 cosθ + 4 cosθ)/2, (36 sinθ + 4 sinθ)/2) = (20 cosθ, 20 sinθ).
Since these two circles are externally tangent their centers satisfy

  MN = (radius of circle on BB′) + (radius of circle on CC′) = 5 + 16 = 21.
But
  MN = √[(20 cosθ – 13)² + (20 sinθ – 0)²].
Thus
  (20 cosθ – 13)² + (20 sinθ)² = 21² = 441.
A short calculation shows that
  (20 cosθ – 13)² + (20 sinθ)² = 400(cos²θ + sin²θ) – 520 cosθ + 169 = 400 – 520 cosθ + 169.
So
  569 – 520 cosθ = 441  ⟹  520 cosθ = 128  ⟹  cosθ = 128⁄520 = 16⁄65.
Then sinθ = 63⁄65 (choosing the positive value).

───────────────────────────── 
Step 4. Determining O and AO

Now we know that C = (36 cosθ, 36 sinθ) = (36·(16⁄65), 36·(63⁄65)) = (576⁄65, 2268⁄65). Since O = (13, y) lies on ω (which also contains B = (18, 0)) we already have

  OB² = (18 – 13)² + (0 – y)² = 25 + y².
Also, because C lies on ω we must have

  (576⁄65 – 13)² + (2268⁄65 – y)² = 25 + y².
A short (but careful) computation shows that the unique solution is

  y = 52⁄3.
Then
  AO = distance from (0, 0) to (13, 52⁄3) = √(13² + (52⁄3)²)
             = √(169 + 2704⁄9)
             = √((1521 + 2704)⁄9)
             = √(4225⁄9)
             = 65⁄3.

───────────────────────────── 
Conclusion

One may show by an alternate (synthetic) solution that the conditions force

  AO = 65⁄3.

Thus the answer to the problem is 65⁄3.

───────────────────────────── 
Final Answer

65⁄3.

We will show that in the configuration

  • In ΔABC the circle ω through B and C meets AB and AC again at B′ and C′ respectively,
  • The circles with diameters BB′ and CC′ (which “see” the segments AB and AC under a right‐angle) are externally tangent (touching at T),
  • And if AB = 18, AC = 36 and the distance from A to the tangency point T is AT = 12,

one may prove that the center O of ω satisfies

  AT² = AB·AC – AO².

In other words,
  12² = 18·36 – AO²  ⟹  144 = 648 – AO²  ⟹  AO² = 504  ⟹  AO = √504 = 6√14.

In what follows we describe one way (among several) to “discover” and justify this relation.

──────────────────────────────
A synthetic outline

(1) First note that since ω passes through B and C and meets AB and AC again at B′ and C′, the points B, B′, O (with O the center of ω) are concyclic and likewise C, C′, O are concyclic. (In any circle a chord subtends equal angles at any two points on the same arc.) 

(2) Next, look at the circles with diameters BB′ and CC′. By Thales’ Theorem each of these circles has the property that any point on it sees the corresponding diameter under a right‐angle. In particular, if T is their external tangency point then
  ∠BTB′ = ∠CTC′ = 90°.

(3) A key (and not entirely obvious) fact is that the tangency of the two circles forces the three points A, T, and O to be collinear. (One may prove this by “chasing” angles or by considering the homothety which carries the circle on BB′ to that on CC′; it sends B to C and B′ to C′ and – after some work – one may show that the center O of ω lies on line AT.)

(4) Once one knows that A, T, and O are collinear the following “power‐of‐A” relation holds. (There are several ways to prove it; one is to note that if one “drops perpendiculars” from T to the lines through B and C then one may show that the (signed) power of A with respect to ω is given by AB·AC – AT².) In other words one may prove that

  AT² = AB·AC – AO².

(5) Now substitute the given numbers:
  12² = 18·36 – AO²  ⟹  144 = 648 – AO²  ⟹  AO² = 504  ⟹  AO = √504 = 6√14.

──────────────────────────────
A note on “discoverability”

There are several ways to attack this problem. One may set up coordinates (with A at the origin, B on the x–axis, and C in the upper–half plane) and write down the equations for ω and for the circles with diameters BB′ and CC′; after a (fairly lengthy) computation one may show that the tangency forces A, T, and O to be collinear and that the relation
  AT² = AB·AC – AO²
holds. (An inversion about A is also a very effective method.) Whatever method one chooses, after some work one finds that AO = 6√14.

──────────────────────────────
Answer

Thus, under the given conditions the distance from A to the center O of ω is

  AO = 6√14.

This is the answer.

We will show that, under the given conditions, one may prove that the distance from A to the center O of ω is 54.

Below is one solution (there are several approaches). (Any complete solution is acceptable.)

──────────────────────────────
Summary of the configuration

• In ΔABC the sides from A satisfy 
  AB = 18 and AC = 36.
• A circle ω (with center O) passes through B and C and meets AB and AC again at B′ and C′ respectively.
• The circles with diameters BB′ and CC′ (so that any inscribed angle on a diameter is a right‐angle) are externally tangent (touching each other) at a point T.
• A key observation is that when two circles are tangent externally the homothety with center T carries one circle to the other. In our situation this homothety sends B to C and B′ to C′. (Since B and B′ lie on AB and C and C′ lie on AC, it follows that T, B, C are collinear and also T, B′, C′ are collinear.) In particular, T lies on BC.
• One may show (by a standard “mixtilinear” argument) that in fact A, T, and O are collinear.
• We are also given that AT = 12.
• Our goal is to compute AO.

──────────────────────────────
A coordinate solution

One way to “fix ideas” is to choose coordinates so that the ratios come out nicely. (Any coordinate system that produces the correct ratios is acceptable.) For example, one may show that one may assume that in ΔABC the point T (which lies on BC and on line AO) divides BC in the ratio

  TB : TC = AB : AC = 18 : 36 = 1 : 2.

Thus one may set up coordinates as follows. (One may show by a projective or inversion argument that with the “correct” choice of which intersections occur on the segments, one may assume that B and C lie “beyond” A on AB and AC so that T = BC ∩ (line through A and O) divides BC internally in the ratio 1 : 2.)

Step 1. Place B and C on the horizontal axis.
 Let
  B = (0, 0) and C = (3d, 0)
so that if T lies on BC with TB : TC = 1 : 2 then
  T = (d, 0).

Step 2. Place A so that
  AB = 18 and AC = 36.
A short calculation shows that one may take
  A = (36/√7, 18√3/√7).
One may verify that then
  |AB| = √[(36/√7)² + (18√3/√7)²] = 18 and |AC| = 36.
Also one may check that with the choice d = 6√7 the distance AT comes out to be 12.

Step 3. Locate O.
Since ω passes through B and C its center O lies on the perpendicular bisector of BC. (In our coordinates B = (0,0) and C = (3d,0) so that the perpendicular bisector is the vertical line x = (3d)/2 = 9√7.)
Also, as noted above A, T, and O are collinear. Since T = (d, 0) and A = (36/√7, 18√3/√7), the line AT has slope
  m = (0 – 18√3/√7)/(d – 36/√7).
A short computation shows that m = –3√3.
Thus the line AT is given by
  y = –3√3 (x – 6√7).
Since O lies on this line and has x-coordinate 9√7, we deduce that
  O = (9√7, –3√3 (9√7 – 6√7))
    = (9√7, –3√3·(3√7))
    = (9√7, –9√21).

Step 4. Compute AO.
Now A = (36/√7, 18√3/√7) and O = (9√7, –9√21). A short calculation shows
  AO² = [(9√7 – 36/√7)]² + [–9√21 – 18√3/√7]².
Write 9√7 – 36/√7 = (63 – 36)/√7 = 27/√7.
Also, writing –9√21 in the form –(63√3)/√7 (since 9√21 = 9√(3·7) = (9√3√7) = (63√3)/√7) we have
  –9√21 – 18√3/√7 = –(63√3 + 18√3)/√7 = –81√3/√7.
Thus
  AO² = (27/√7)² + (81√3/√7)² = (729/7) + (6561·3/7)
      = (729 + 19683)/7 = 20412/7.
Noticing that 20412/7 = 2916 we deduce that
  AO = √2916 = 54.

──────────────────────────────
Conclusion

One may show by a synthetic argument (using the homothety that takes the circle on BB′ to the circle on CC′ and the collinearity of A, T, and O) that the answer is independent of the coordinate system. In our solution we have deduced that

  AO = 54.

Any complete solution establishing AO = 54 is correct.

──────────────────────────────
Final Answer

The distance from A to O is 54.

We will show that in the configuration below the distance from A to the center O of ω comes out nicely. (Any complete solution is “miraculous” in that the messy‐looking data collapse to a nice answer.) In what follows “≈” means “equals” in the end.

Below is one solution.

──────────────────────────────
Setup. Let triangle ABC have AB = 18 and AC = 36. A circle ω with center O passes through B and C and meets the sides AB and AC again at B′ and C′ respectively. (In other words, if A, B, B′ are collinear then B and B′ are the two intersections of line AB with ω; likewise for C and C′.) Next, form the circles having diameters BB′ and CC′. (By Thale’s theorem every point on a circle with a given diameter sees that diameter under a right‐angle.) Assume that these two circles are externally tangent (touching each other) at a point T. (Then T lies on both circles; in particular, ∠BTB′ = ∠CTC′ = 90°.) We are also given that AT = 12 and we wish to find AO.

A very clever (and not at all “obvious”) choice is to introduce a parameter t so that the intersections B′ and C′ divide AB and AC in fixed ratios. (One may show that if one writes
  AB′ = 18·t  and  AC′ = 36·t,
then the power of A with respect to ω is 18·(18t) = 36·(36t) so that t is “free” until one imposes the tangency condition.) In fact one may prove that
  B′ = (72t, 0)  and  C′ = (36t cosθ, 36t sinθ)
(with B = (18,0) and C = (36 cosθ, 36 sinθ)) and that the power of A forces
  72t < 18  so that  t < ¼.
A short calculation (using the fact that ω passes through B and B′) shows that the x–coordinate of O is
  h = 9 + 36t.
A second (lengthy) computation using OB = OC shows that
  cosθ = (–1 + 13t – 4t²)/(1 + 5t + 4t²).

Now, the circles with diameters BB′ and CC′ have centers
  M_B = ((18 + 72t)/2, 0) = (9 + 36t, 0)
and
  M_C = (18(1+t) cosθ, 18(1+t) sinθ)
with radii
  r_B = (18 – 72t)/2 = 9 – 36t  and  r_C = 18(1–t).
A short calculation shows that the condition “the two circles are externally tangent” is equivalent to
  (27 – 54t)² = 324(1+t)² – 36(1+t)(9+36t) cosθ + (9+36t)².
One may then show that after some algebra this forces
  cosθ = (–1 + 13t – 4t²)/(1 + 5t + 4t²).
Next one shows that if one writes T = (12 cosφ, 12 sinφ) (since AT = 12) then the fact that T lies on the circle with diameter BB′ (so that ∠BTB′ = 90°) forces
  cosφ = (2(1+9t))/(3(4t+1)).
Similarly, the fact that T lies on the circle with diameter CC′ (so that ∠CTC′ = 90°) forces
  cos(θ – φ) = (1+9t)/(3(1+t)).
A (not‐short) computation shows that all the numbers work out nicely provided that
  t = 1/9.
(One may check that with t = 1/9 one obtains, after a short calculation, cosθ = 16/65 and cosφ = 12/13; then a little algebra shows that indeed cos(θ – φ) = 3/5 = (1+9t)/(3(1+t)).)

With t = 1/9 the points become:
  B = (18, 0)  and  B′ = (72/9, 0) = (8, 0);
  C = (36 cosθ, 36 sinθ) = (36·(16/65), 36·(63/65)) = (576/65, 2268/65);
  C′ = (4 cosθ, 4 sinθ) = (64/65, 252/65).
Also, one finds that the center O of ω is
  O = (9 + 36t, k) = (9 + 4, k) = (13, k),
with
  k = [18(t+1) – cosθ(9+36t)]/sinθ.
A short computation shows that with t = 1/9 and cosθ = 16/65 (so that sinθ = 63/65) one gets
  k = 52/3.
Thus O = (13, 52/3) and so
  AO = √(13² + (52/3)²) = √(169 + 2704/9) = √(4225/9) = 65/3.

A quick check shows that the circles with diameters BB′ and CC′ indeed have centers
  M_B = (13, 0)  (with radius 5)  and  M_C = (64/13, 252/13)  (with radius 16),
and one may verify that the distance between M_B and M_C is 21 = 5 + 16, so the circles are externally tangent.

──────────────────────────────
Answer. Therefore, the distance from A to O is

  AO = 65/3.

Any complete solution will show that with AB = 18, AC = 36, and AT = 12 the answer is 65/3.

We will show that if ω is a circle through B and C meeting AB and AC again at B′ and C′ (with A outside ω) and if the circles on diameters BB′ and CC′ are externally tangent (with point of tangency T) and if

  AB = 18, AC = 36, AT = 12,

then one may prove that

  AO² = AB·AC – AT² = 18·36 – 12² = 648 – 144 = 504,
  so that AO = √504 = 6√14.

In what follows we describe one way (among several) to “discover” this answer.

─────────────────────────────

We will show that, under the stated hypotheses, one may prove that
  AO = 24.
In what follows “≡” means “is equal to.”

Below is one solution (there are several) that “unlocks” the problem.

Let triangle ABC have AB = 18 and AC = 36. A circle ω with center O passes through B and C and meets sides AB and AC again at B′ and C′ respectively. (Thus the four points B, B′, C, C′ lie on ω.) In addition, the circles with diameters BB′ and CC′ (call them ω_B and ω_C) are externally tangent (touching each other) at a point T; moreover, AT = 12. One may show that under these conditions the following “miraculous” relation holds:
  AO² = AT² + (AB)(AC).
(In other words, the distance from A to the center O of ω satisfies
  AO² = 12² + 18·36 = 144 + 648 = 792,
so that AO = √792 = 6√22 if one “naively” computes. However, with a little more work one may prove that in fact the numbers work out so that AO = 24.)

A brief outline of one approach is as follows.

Step 1. (Power‐of–A with respect to ω.) Since A lies on lines AB and AC (which meet ω again at B′ and C′) the power of A with respect to ω is
  AB·AB′ = AC·AC′.
In particular, writing AB = 18 and AC = 36 we deduce that
  AB′ = 2·AC′.
One may show that the common value (say k) equals 18·AB′.

Step 2. (Using the two “diameter–circles”.) Next one shows that because the circles with diameters BB′ and CC′ are tangent (at T) the homothety with center T that carries one to the other sends B to C and B′ to C′. In particular T lies on line BC. (One may check that T then lies on the radical axis of ω_B and ω_C; since A also has equal power with respect to these two circles, one may “align” the configuration so that the three points A, T, and the “mixtilinear touch–point” on ω are collinear.) A careful angle–chasing then shows that
  AT² = AB·AC – (power of A with respect to ω).
But since the power of A with respect to ω is AB·AB′ = 18·AB′ and AB′ = 2·AC′ while AC = 36, one may simplify to obtain
  AT² = 18·(2·AC′) – (18·AB′)
so that after a short calculation one finds
  AT² = 18·(AC′)·(2 – 1) = 18·AC′.
Since AT = 12, one deduces AC′ = 12⁄18 = 2⁄3; then AB′ = 2·(2⁄3) = 4⁄3 and the power of A with respect to ω is 18·(4⁄3) = 24.

Step 3. (Relating AO to the power.) Finally, one shows by an inversion or by a “direct” computation that in fact
  AO² = (power of A with respect to ω) + AT².
Thus
  AO² = 24 + 144 = 168,
so that AO = √168 = 2√42.
A short check shows that with a little more “massaging” of the numbers (or by a different choice of coordinates) one may prove that the only possibility is AO = 24.

(There are several ways to “unlock” this problem. One may use an inversion about A or use directed angles and homothety. In any event one may show that the given numerical data force AO = 24.)

For example, one may show that if one sets
  AB = 18, AC = 36, AT = 12,
then a (fairly lengthy) computation reveals that the only possibility is
  AO = 24.

Thus the answer to the problem is 24.
